sp500_trend.why: The index against its own 10-month average price. A month-end close below that line means selling has outlasted a normal pullback, which is how broad market downturns have usually shown up in monthly prices.
sp500_trend.record: Lagging: held the 2000-02 and 2007-09 losses under 4%, but 52 of 56 exits since 1950 were false alarms.

yield_curve.why: The gap between 10-year and 3-month Treasury yields. When short rates exceed long rates (an inversion), markets expect the economy to weaken, which has often come before recessions and equity peaks.
yield_curve.record: Inverted about 15 months before the October 2007 peak and had re-steepened by it. False alarms in 2019 and 2022-24 (780 days inverted, no recession). Nothing signaled in 1987.

baa_spread.why: The extra yield on Baa-rated corporate bonds, the lowest investment-grade tier, over 10-year Treasuries. It widens when lenders start to doubt ordinary companies can repay, which tends to precede or accompany equity declines.
baa_spread.record: Widened about 58 bp in the two months before the 2000 peak and began widening about 3 months before 2007. False alarms in 2011, 2014-16, 2018 and 2025.

hy_oas.why: Extra yield investors demand on junk bonds (below investment grade). It widens when credit stress spreads beyond the weakest borrowers; it was tight at both the 2000 and 2007 peaks and widened only after.
hy_oas.record: Tight at both peaks; spiked to about 8-9% in 2011 and 2016 with no recession (secondary source). FRED carries only three years of history for free.

claims.why: Weekly new unemployment insurance filings, averaged over four weeks and compared with the lowest level of the past year. A sustained jump means layoffs are rising, a late-stage sign that a slowdown has begun.
claims.record: Lagging: crossed 20% about 8 months after the 2000 peak and 6 months after 2007. False alarms from hurricanes in 2005 and 2017, and in 2023.

sahm.why: A recession gauge built from the unemployment rate: how far its three-month average has risen above its lowest point of the past year. At 0.50 points or more, a recession has usually begun.
sahm.record: Lagging: fired 15 months after the 2000 peak and 6 months after 2007. False trigger in 2024.

fed_path.why: The Fed's policy interest rate and which way it last moved. It is context, not a trigger, because market peaks have tended to come while rates were rising or just after cuts began.
fed_path.record: Every peak since 1987 came during tightening or just after the turn to easing. A regime guide, not a timer.

ai_credit.why: Stress in the debt of companies funding AI buildouts. Oracle's credit default swap (CDS) price is the cost of insuring its bonds against default; CoreWeave's bond prices show how lenders value the riskiest AI borrower.
ai_credit.record: No long history. Modeled on the 2000-01 telecom debt repricing, when credit stress hit the funders of network buildouts.

hyperscaler_capex.why: Spending plans of the biggest cloud companies (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta) on data centers and chips. Their spending is the revenue for the AI supply chain, so cuts would hit demand directly.
hyperscaler_capex.record: No long history. Judgment-call trigger modeled on 2001, when telecom capital spending cuts hit equipment makers hard.

ai_lab_funding.why: Whether AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic can still raise money at rising valuations and list on public markets. A lower-priced funding round or pulled IPO would signal the window is closing.
ai_lab_funding.record: No long history. Judgment-call trigger modeled on the IPO window closing in 2000.

dram_prices.why: Contract prices for DRAM, the memory chips in AI servers. Memory stocks usually fall before prices do; falling contract prices would mean AI hardware demand is cooling.
dram_prices.record: Memory equities led contract prices by 3 to 9 months in 2018 and 2022.

gpu_rental.why: What it costs to rent an Nvidia H100 graphics chip, the workhorse of AI training. Falling rental prices would mean AI computing capacity is outrunning demand.
gpu_rental.record: No long history. Modeled on the 2001 bandwidth price collapse, when overbuilt capacity pushed prices down sharply.

lease_cancellations.why: Reports that cloud companies are canceling data center leases. Large cancellations would be an early sign that planned AI capacity is more than they expect to need.
lease_cancellations.record: A February 2025 Microsoft report of canceled leases (a couple hundred megawatts) was a false alarm.

earnings_revisions.why: Whether analysts are raising or cutting profit forecasts for S&P 500 companies. Prices ultimately follow earnings, so months of net downward revisions would suggest the market's growth expectations are too high.
earnings_revisions.record: Shown for context; not part of the AI count. Treated as a confirming signal, not an early warning.

tsmc_revenue.why: Monthly sales of TSMC, the maker of most advanced AI chips. Strong growth means chip orders from AI customers are still rising; a sharp slowdown would show demand fading.
tsmc_revenue.record: Coincident at best: revenue stayed strong after the January 2022 equity peak.
